newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda genocide suspects plead not guilty.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda genocide suspects plead not guilty.

text.p: Two former senior Rwandan officials pleaded not guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity in their first appearances on Wednesday before the troubled U.N. tribunal into 1994's mass slaughter.

Anatole Nsengiyumva, a colonel in the former Rwandan army, and Ferdinand Nahimana, a former director of extremist Radio Milles Collines (RTLM), appeared separately before the tribunal in north Tanzania.
They were the most senior former officials to plead but will be followed on Thursday by former colonel Theoneste Bagosora, widely considered the most wanted genocide suspect detained.
The three-judge court met in closed hearings to set dates for their respective trials after the two pleaded not guilty.
The court appearances follow a scathing U.N. report last week on the operations of the international tribunal and its officials.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Friday meets Chief Prosecutor Louise Arbor of Canada, Deputy Prosecutor Honore Rakotomanana of Madagascar and Registrar Andronico Adede of Kenya in New York.

Annan has vowed to discipline officials if necessary after the U.N. report following a two-month investigation detailed gross mismanagement and financial incompetence at the tribunal and said not one administrative area functioned effectively.

The report by Karl Paschke, a German diplomat who heads the U.N. Office of Internal Oversight Services, was most harsh on alleged abuses in Adede's department but did not recommend he should be dismissed.
Bagosora, accused of directing events during the first few days of the genocide, and Andre Ntagerura, a former minister of transport, appear on Thursday before the court which will set trial dates.

A prosecution indictment charged Nsengiyumva on Wednesday with four counts of direct and public incitement to genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of Article Three of the Geneva Conventions.
Nsengiyumva's men killed a Tutsi father with machetes and severely injured his son after they failed to comply with an order to get into his truck, according to the indictment.
He also ordered the killing of Tutsi civilians during a meeting in Gisenyi prefecture, the prosecution said.

Nahimana was charged with the same crimes as Nsengiyumva and exercised direct control over RTLM used to broadcast messages inciting the population to kill Tutsis and political opponents of the regime, it said.

"Ferdinand Nahimana knew or had reason to know that his subordinates in RTLM had faciliated and or broadcast such broadcasts and failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such broadcasts," the indictment said.

An estimated 800,000 members of the Tutsi minority and Hutu moderates were slaughtered between April and July 1994 by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs following the killing of Rwanda's Hutu president.
A total of 21 suspects have been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which was set up in 1994 to bring to justice architects of the genocide.

The trial of former mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu started in January. The tribunal can impose a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in contrast to Rwandan courts which have sentenced more than 10 defendants to death since December for genocide.
